lessons.title: Cancelling Before They Charge Me Again

script.speaker: Member
script.line: Hi, I'd like to cancel my membership, my next billing date is in four days and I want to make sure it's done in time.

script.speaker: Staff
script.line: Sure, I can help with that. Can I ask what's prompting the cancellation?

script.speaker: Member
script.line: Honestly, I just haven't been going, life's been busy and it's not worth forty-five dollars a month right now.

script.speaker: Staff
script.line: Totally get that. Just so you know, we do offer a freeze option, three months for ten dollars a month if you think you might come back.

script.speaker: Member
script.line: That's tempting, but I'd rather just cancel clean for now.

script.speaker: Staff
script.line: No worries, I can process that. There's a fourteen-day notice period though, so your final charge will be next month's bill.

script.speaker: Member
script.line: Wait, so I'll still get charged even though I'm cancelling today?

script.speaker: Staff
script.line: Yeah, unfortunately it's in the contract, cancellations need two weeks notice, so one more payment goes through.

script.speaker: Member
script.line: That's a bit annoying, but I guess that's fair since I did sign up for it.

script.speaker: Staff
script.line: I appreciate you understanding. After that charge, no further payments will come out.

script.speaker: Member
script.line: Okay, and will I get a confirmation email for this?

script.speaker: Staff
script.line: Yes, you'll get one within the hour with your cancellation date confirmed.

script.speaker: Member
script.line: Perfect, thanks for making this painless at least.

script.speaker: Advisor
script.line: Hi, thanks for booking this session, I understand you're torn between two programs?

script.speaker: Student
script.line: Yeah, exactly, I got into both the business program and the computer science one, and I honestly can't decide.

script.speaker: Advisor
script.line: Okay, let's break it down. What's drawing you to each one?

script.speaker: Student
script.line: Business feels safer, like I know what I'm getting into, but computer science pays better from what I've heard.

script.speaker: Advisor
script.line: That's generally true, entry-level salaries in tech tend to run higher, though it varies a lot by specialization.

script.speaker: Student
script.line: Right, but I'm worried I'll struggle since I've never coded before.

script.speaker: Advisor
script.line: That's a fair concern, but the program's designed for beginners, first year is pretty foundational.

script.speaker: Student
script.line: Okay, that's reassuring actually. What about workload, is one noticeably harder than the other?

script.speaker: Advisor
script.line: Computer science tends to have a heavier workload, especially second and third year, lots of late nights debugging.

script.speaker: Student
script.line: Ha, sounds rough. Is there any option to switch later if I start in one and it's not for me?

script.speaker: Advisor
script.line: Yeah, actually quite a few students switch between the two after first year since there's overlap in some courses.

script.speaker: Student
script.line: Oh, that changes things, I didn't realize that was even possible.

script.speaker: Advisor
script.line: It is, as long as your grades meet the minimum threshold, usually around a seventy percent average.

script.speaker: Student
script.line: Okay, that gives me a bit more breathing room to just pick one and see how it goes.

script.speaker: Advisor
script.line: Exactly, and remember, you're not locking yourself into a career forever, just a starting point.

script.speaker: Student
script.line: That's a good way to look at it. I think I'll go with computer science then, and keep business as a backup mentally.
